artists.biography:
John William Coltrane (also known as "Trane"; September 23, 1926 – July 17, 1967) was an American jazz saxophonist and composer. Working in the bebop and hard bop idioms early in his career, Coltrane helped pioneer the use of modes in jazz and later was at the forefront of free jazz. He organized at least fifty recording sessions as a leader during his recording career, and appeared as a sideman on many other albums, notably with trumpeter Miles Davis and pianist Thelonious Monk.
As his career progressed, Coltrane and his music took on an increasingly spiritual dimension. His second wife was pianist Alice Coltrane and their son Ravi Coltrane is a saxophonist. Coltrane influenced innumerable musicians, and remains one of the most significant saxophonists in jazz history. He received many posthumous awards and recognitions, including canonization by the African Orthodox Church as Saint John William Coltrane. In 2007, Coltrane was awarded the Pulitzer Prize Special Citation for his "masterful improvisation, supreme musicianship and iconic centrality to the history of jazz."

lastfm.wiki_content: Olé Coltrane is an album by jazz musician John Coltrane released in November 1961 on Atlantic Records (SD 1373). The album was recorded at A&R Studios in New York (May 1961), and was the last of Coltrane's Atlantic albums to be made under his own supervision. Recording Two days prior to recording Olé Coltrane, John Coltrane had completed Africa/Brass, his first session for Impulse! Records, at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. Still under contract to Atlantic for one remaining album, he returned to the studio with his working quintet and expanded the lineup by adding Art Davis and Freddie Hubbard, both participants in the earlier Africa/Brass date. Due to his existing contractual obligations with Prestige Records, Eric Dolphy was credited on the album under the pseudonym George Lane. Coltrane’s exploration of Spanish musical elements on the title track “Olé” may have been influenced by Miles Davis’s Sketches of Spain, released the previous year. The modal structure of “Olé” draws from the traditional folk melody “El Vito,” later associated with “El Quinto Regimiento,” while Coltrane’s soprano saxophone playing recalls his earlier work on My Favorite Things. The compositions on side two continue the group’s interest in African musical forms, an approach developed during the May 23 Africa/Brass sessions. McCoy Tyner later explained that “Dahomey Dance” was inspired by rhythmic patterns Coltrane had encountered in recordings of musicians from Dahomey, which influenced the decision to feature two bassists. Tyner’s ballad “Aisha” was named after his then-wife. Personnel: John Coltrane — soprano saxophone on Olé; tenor saxophone on Dahomey Dance & AishaFreddie Hubbard — trumpetEric Dolphy — flute on Olé; alto saxophone on Dahomey Dance & AishaMcCoy Tyner — pianoReggie Workman — bassArt Davis — bass on Olé & Dahomey DanceElvin Jones — drums Read more on Last.fm. perplexity.description:
Olé Coltrane is a pivotal late-Atlantic John Coltrane album, recorded in 1961 and released later that year as his final studio statement for the label. Built around a long, modal title track, it finds Coltrane stretching beyond hard bop into a more expansive, rhythmically adventurous language that was becoming central to his art. The album’s Spanish-flavored atmosphere on “Olé” gives way to the more searching and spacious interplay of “Dahomey Dance” and “Aisha,” with the sessions also reflecting the transitional lineup Coltrane was using at the time, including Eric Dolphy, McCoy Tyner, Reggie Workman, and Elvin Jones.

The record is widely regarded as one of the key bridges between Coltrane’s early 1960s Atlantic work and the more exploratory music he would make soon after for Impulse!. Its blend of melodic discipline, modal construction, and free-leaning improvisation helped define his mature style, while the session’s ensemble sound captures both power and tension. As a whole, Olé Coltrane stands as an essential jazz document: concise compared with Coltrane’s later epics, but already audacious in scope and unmistakably forward-looking.
